documents.abstract: ABSTRACT This review examines how computational medicinal chemistry has transformed drug repurposing and bioactivity optimization for rare and emerging diseases over the 2021–2026 period. Conventional de novo drug discovery remains costly and slow typically requiring more than one billion dollars and 10–17 years failing to adequately serve the over 300 million people living with rare diseases, 95% of whom lack approved treatments. Drug repurposing offers an attractive alternative by leveraging established safety, pharmacokinetic, and manufacturing profiles. Computational approaches are integral to this strategy: target‐based methods (e.g., molecular docking) supply mechanistic insights; ligand‐based methods (e.g., QSAR) enable screening without solved target structures; network‐based approaches integrate multi‐omics data; and artificial intelligence enhances predictive accuracy across all three domains. Key developments include pharmacological chaperones for Fabry disease, allosteric regulators for mucopolysaccharidosis type I, and computationally nominated COVID‐19 therapeutics. Major challenges include inconsistent datasets, limited docking accuracy, qualitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) overfitting, and a persistent translational gap. Closing this validation gap through data standardization, rigorous prospective testing, and multidisciplinary collaboration is essential if computational predictions are to yield safe, effective therapies for unmet clinical needs.

Language model pipelines extract multi-dimensional factor vectors from financial text, but a trading desk needs to know when an extracted vector can be trusted. Audit labels arrive late, errors cluster in stress regimes, and error scale shifts after model or prompt updates. We evaluate a conformal gate on the extraction layer in a seeded simulation (300 firms, 60 quarters, 200 replications) with heavy-tailed errors, regime stress, a structural break and a two-quarter audit lag. Per-dimension 90% intervals cover the full eight-dimension vector only 43 to 48% of the time, while a max-score construction reaches 89.8% before the break with intervals 20 to 26% narrower than Bonferroni. Calibration frozen at go-live falls to 79.9% joint coverage after the break. Rolling, weighted and delayed-feedback adaptive calibration recover 88.2 to 89.8% on average, but no label-driven method protects the quarters just after a shift. As a risk control, the gate holds the error rate among accepted signals near 10% after the break, the adaptive protocols accept only 25 to 35% of signals, and the gate lowers risk-adjusted return in this design. As a risk control, the adaptive gates reject most signals after the break, accepting only 25 to 35% in the main study, and gating lowers risk-adjusted return in this design. A label-free drift monitor flags 83.5% of abrupt breaks in the quarter they occur, against 2.5% for label-based monitoring, but under gradual drift it flags only 3.5%, so its advantage but in the supplementary simulation code, where it flags 78.5% of abrupt breaks, it flags only 3.5% under gradual drift, so its advantage is specific to abrupt breaks. To test whether these mechanisms appear with a real extractor, we run a pilot that extracts seven financial fields from the earnings press releases of 492 S&P 500 companies the earnings press releases of 492 large US companies from an S&P 500 earnings-call dataset with an open-weight model and scores each figure against the SEC XBRL-reported value. Extraction is accurate for most figures, 94.9% within 1% once reference-label errors in the XBRL tags are corrected, and most of the figures first scored as errors turned out to be label errors rather than misreading. Extraction is accurate for most figures, 95.5% within 1% once an error in our choice of revenue tag for the reference labels is corrected, and about a quarter of the figures first scored as large errors turned out to be label errors rather than misreading. The model's own GAAP flag is constant and detects none of the errors, while cross-model disagreement detects a minority of them, which supports the paper's central claim that a usable confidence signal must come from an external check rather than the model's own output. The one self-reported signal collected, the model's GAAP flag, is constant and uninformative, while disagreement across three models detects 45% of the large errors at the cost of flagging 8.6% of correct figures, which is consistent with the view that a usable confidence signal must come from a check outside a single model's output, although richer self-reported signals were not tested. A Monte Carlo simulation calibrated to the pilot reproduces these rates at scale. A Monte Carlo resampling calibrated to the pilot, with the detector's operating point held fixed, gives sampling intervals for the accuracy and large-error rates. The results support three design rules: The results suggest three design rules: report joint reliability with a max-score rectangle, gate on the composite the operator consumes, and size positions by a smoothed scale rather than by calibrated width. We place the gate in a deployment framework and state its limits.

Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) and cyber-physical control systems deployed in mission-critical environments present severe operational risks due to stochastic hallucinations, non-deterministic drift, and a lack of hard formal safety guarantees. Concurrently, theoretical breakthroughs in harmonic analysis -specifically OpenAI’s 2026 proof of Sogge’s local smoothing conjecture for the Euclidean wave equation (n ≥ 2) - have established continuous analytical bounds on wave focusing and energy concentration in Lp Sobolev spaces. In this monograph, we present a unified Data Physics framework bridging continuous Sobolev local smoothing with the discrete Layer 0 Invariant State Matrix (L0-ISM) architecture. We formalize the Helical Venturi Operator (Φv), which dynamically constricts logit sampling spaces based on Shannon entropy H(Pt), and map continuous boundary conditions onto a symmetric 19-state bounded lattice S ∈ {-9, ..., 0, ..., +9}. Using an embedded Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT Z3 / CP-SAT) formal solver, we prove that quantized state trajectories can be formally verified in sub-millisecond latency (<0.35 ms). Any physical invariant violation or boundary saturation (|si| ≥ 9) triggers an immediate, deterministic hardware-level -999 HARD_STOP interdiction. We demonstrate that L0-ISM provides an unbreachable safety envelope for real-time AI and critical infrastructure (e.g., mCDU cooling loops), eliminating matrix-lag and replacing soft prompt heuristics with mathematical certainty.

ABSTRACT Controlling shareholder share pledging exposes the controlling shareholder to the risk of losing corporate control in the event of a stock price decline. This paper aims to examine whether controlling shareholder share pledging drives corporate AI washing, and to identify the mechanisms through which this effect operates. This study indicates that controlling shareholder share pledging exerts a significant and robust exacerbating effect on corporate AI washing. The mechanism through which this effect operates lies in heightened earnings aggressiveness and aggravated information opacity. Besides, agency problems significantly strengthen this positive relationship, as controlling shareholders with greater agency discretion face fewer internal constraints on opportunistic AI disclosures. Analyst coverage, however, attenuates this exacerbating effect, consistent with the view that external monitoring by information intermediaries disciplines controlling shareholders' opportunistic behavior and mitigates the informational consequences of share pledging. From the perspective of controlling shareholders' financing behavior, this paper examines the driving effect of share pledging on corporate AI washing through heightened earnings aggressiveness and aggravated information opacity, thereby introducing this emerging opportunistic practice into the literature on the real effects of share pledging. Meanwhile, agency problems reinforce this effect from the internal governance perspective, while analyst coverage attenuates it from the external monitoring perspective, providing practical insights for regulators and investors to curb AI washing through the integration of internal and external governance mechanisms.

In India, traditionally made wooden toys are valuable for child safety and are eco-friendly. The study shows prototyping with design analysis. It considers wooden toys as expressive, eco-friendly products. It will help the environment and empower artisans. Encouraging heritage preservation, sustainability, and innovation in the toy industry and avoiding plastic. This paper focuses on the gap found during this research. The quantity production of wooden toys gets an average response in their creative and cultural potential, using Sawant Wadi as an example. As plastic toys are in demand in production, it analyzes the industrial preparation and chance of creativity, and demand for a new design with modularity, better usability, and rich in symbolic meaning.

Forest and land fires require leadership, interorganizational coordination, information management, resource mobilization, and community participation. Yet research on wildfire leadership, cross-jurisdictional collaboration, firefighter safety, and forest-and-land-fire governance differs in context, unit of analysis, and outcome measures, which limits comparability. This article presents a systematic literature review of 51 studies published in 2015–2026 (43 core and 8 comparator articles), selected from 447 Scopus records (440 after deduplication) records and reported following PRISMA 2020. The literature is mapped with the Theory–Context–Characteristics–Methods (TCCM) framework and synthesized with the Antecedents–Decisions/Practices–Outcomes (ADO) framework. In the response phase, the most widely coded themes are strategic communication and shared situational awareness (22 articles) and cross-actor coordination and resource negotiation (20 articles). The most widely coded constraint is resource scarcity, time pressure, workload, and fatigue (23 articles), while open information flow and negotiated interdependence each appear as supporting factors in 19 articles. These counts indicate thematic coverage, not effect sizes or causal evidence. The review identifies nine gaps, chiefly the need to link leader competencies and governance conditions to collaborative mechanisms and to operational, safety, and socio-ecological outcomes; to understand power asymmetries; and to test the transferability of wildfire models to Indonesia. The article proposes an integrative ADO model and nine propositions for comparative, longitudinal, and mixed-methods research.

Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support academic performance while also creating a perceived gap between AI-supported task completion and independently available competence. This study examined how multidimensional critical thinking dispositions are associated with cognitive offloading, cognitive enhancement, and perceived support-dependence discrepancy (PSD) in GenAI-assisted learning. Methods A cross-sectional survey was administered through Wenjuanxing from March 15 to May 20, 2026, using stratified purposive sampling across six Chinese universities. Of 990 submitted questionnaires, 797 eligible and complete responses were retained. The hypothesized pathways were tested using structural equation modeling, with a separate observed-score moderation analysis for academic stress and additional robustness and measurement-model assessments. Results Inquisitiveness was positively associated with cognitive enhancement (β = 0.515, p < 0.001) and cognitive offloading (β = 0.270, p < 0.001). Open-mindedness (β = 0.091, p = 0.039) and systematicity (β = 0.096, p = 0.029) showed small positive associations with cognitive enhancement, whereas analyticity and truth-seeking were not significantly associated with either interaction pathway. Cognitive offloading (β = 0.448, p < 0.001) and cognitive enhancement (β = 0.207, p < 0.001) were positively associated with PSD. The Academic Stress × Cognitive Offloading interaction was not significant (β = 0.048, p = 0.123; delta R-squared = 0.002). Alternative CFA specifications, a common-method-factor analysis, and reliability sensitivity analyses yielded broadly consistent focal conclusions, while the HTMT assessment provided qualified evidence of discriminant validity. Conclusion Critical thinking dispositions showed heterogeneous associations with GenAI interaction pathways, and both offloading and enhancement were associated with perceived support-dependent competence gaps. Because the outcome was measured with a single self-report item and the design was cross-sectional, the findings indicate statistical associations rather than objectively verified overconfidence, calibration bias, or causal effects.

The paper introduces a new Cross-Domain Knowledge Retrieval Framework that is aimed at optimizing dispatching of power in the current electricity grids. The framework combines Large Language Models (LLMs) with hybrid vectors-relational databases to use structured and unstructured data to make better decisions. Conventional grid management systems usually operate with limited datasets and invariable models and this may lead to inefficient power generation, high operation cost and poor grid stability. Conversely, the proposed system works with various sources of data, such as live grid load data, energy prices, and weather projections to provide adaptable and cost-efficient solutions to dynamic power dispatching. The framework is able to maximize power production and distribution by integrating advanced machine learning algorithms with real-time data, with a particular emphasis on maximizing the use of renewable sources and reducing the use of costly, non-renewable ones. It uses deep reinforcement learning, semantic search to process unstructured data, including weather report and operational logs, in addition to conventional structured data (e.g., market data and grid status). This system is integrated to enable it to make real-time changes depending on the changing conditions of demand and generation so as to achieve the best grid stability and efficient use of the available resources. The numerical analysis system performance shows that the system has significantly improved compared to the literature methods. It is shown that the Proposed System will result in a 90% reduction in costs, a 95% decrease in energy consumption, and a 95% improvement in grid stability and a response time of 0.05 seconds. Compared to such methods as Knowledge Graph-based Dispatch, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), and Distributed Optimization, the Proposed System is better in all the most important performance metrics. It is the best at real-time decision-making, dynamic optimization, and the overall efficiency of the grid, providing the highest performance regarding the reduction of costs, energy efficiency, and grid stability. The suggested structure is a scaled and flexible approach to managing the power grid in the future, especially in situations when it is crucial to combine renewable energy, make the grid run in real-time, and achieve cost reduction at the same time to keep the grid balanced and cause the least harm to the environment.

Background Large language models (LLMs) are capable of providing health information and consultation to patients with osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH). However, owing to imbalances in the linguistic distribution of their training corpora, the quality, readability, and safety profiles of outputs generated by the same model may vary across language settings. Objective This study aimed to compare bilingual responses to ONFH patient queries generated by six state-of-the-art flagship LLMs, comprising three English-oriented models (ChatGPT-5.6-Sol, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and Claude-Fable-5) and three Chinese-oriented models (DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Qwen3.7-Max, and Doubao-Seed-2.1-Pro), and to multidimensionally evaluate their cross-linguistic capabilities for generating medical information in terms of information quality, actionability, clinical accuracy, safety risk, hallucination, and readability. Methods A question set comprising 36 semantically distinct patient queries regarding ONFH was developed, yielding 72 semantically matched English–Chinese paired prompts. Six state-of-the-art flagship LLMs were evaluated. Information quality was assessed using the Global Quality Score (GQS), DISCERN, the Quality Assessment of Medical Artificial Intelligence (QAMAI), and the 20-item Ensuring Quality Information for Patients (EQIP-20). Actionability was assessed using the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials (PEMAT-P), while clinical accuracy was evaluated using a 5-point Likert scale. Safety risk was assessed using a graded classification framework, and prespecified criteria were established for identifying hallucinations. Readability was evaluated using language-specific readability metrics for English and Chinese responses. Statistical analyses included the Friedman test, paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and Spearman correlation analysis. Results A total of 432 responses generated by LLMs were included in this study, and good-to-excellent inter-rater reliability was observed for all evaluation indicators. Significant between-model differences in actionability and clinical accuracy were identified among the six models under both English and Chinese response conditions (all p < 0.05). Furthermore, clinical accuracy exhibited high cross-linguistic stability. ChatGPT-5.6-Sol showed high actionability and a relatively low frequency of Level 1 minor safety-related omissions under the English-language condition, whereas switching to Chinese was accompanied by reduced actionability and an increased frequency of Level 1 omissions. All observed nonzero safety events were Level 1 minor omissions; no Level 2 or Level 3 unsafe responses were identified in either language condition. Responses generated by all six models in both languages failed to reach the prespecified readability threshold for patient education. Conclusion The six LLMs showed significant inter-model differences in the actionability and clinical accuracy of responses to ONFH-related patient health queries in both English and Chinese settings, while clinical accuracy demonstrated favorable cross-linguistic stability. Notably, none of the six-model outputs met the applicable readability threshold for patient-targeted health education under either language condition. In clinical practice, model selection, prompting-language effects and hallucination-related risks should be comprehensively considered when deploying LLMs to deliver health information for patients with ONFH. At the present stage, LLM-generated content intended for direct patient-facing education requires cautious evaluation and human oversight.

documents.abstract: In order to solve the problem of cross-scene semantic drift of accounting English terms, this study constructs a multi-dimensional space of “scene semantics” and formalizes semantic drift into probability distribution transformation. An improved BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers)-Attention model integrating gated attention mechanism and Kullback-Leibler divergence is developed and the semantic drift flux index is proposed to quantitatively measure the drift degree. This paper further designs a two-tier standardization mechanism of “Simhash coarse screening+BERT fine matching” and a human-machine cooperation workflow of “Artificial Intelligence early warning expert judgment”. This method realizes the quantitative management of semantic drift of accounting terms, enhances the international comparability of accounting information, and promotes the transformation of accounting linguistics to computational social science paradigm. Through real-time terminology governance, the framework reduces the burden of manual audit of accounting supervision institutions and reduces compliance risks.

Abstract Background Subcutaneous oncology monoclonal antibodies (SCOmAbs) offer significant benefits compared to intravenous formulations, including reduced administration time and potential for self-administration. However, little has been published on real-world preparation and administration practices with these novel formulations. Methods This was a qualitative, exploratory study of 30 participants (10 patients receiving SCOmAbs, 10 nurses, and 10 pharmacists/pharmacy technicians) across various U.S. healthcare facilities. One-on-one, in-depth interviews examined current practices, pain points, device integration potential, projected impact of increased SCOmAb adoption, and perspectives on home administration. Results Findings revealed considerable variability in SCOmAb preparation and administration practices. While preparation methods generally aligned with typical parenteral workflows, notable deviations included bedside preparation by nurses (7/30), use of syringe pump modules (3/19), and one case of patient self-administration at home. Most participants utilized closed-system transfer devices (12/22) despite inconsistent hazardous drug treatment between facilities. Administration challenges included ergonomic difficulties for nurses during manual push (5/9 reporting physical discomfort) and variable injection techniques to accommodate patient comfort. Nurses reported significant workflow impact from being “tethered” to patients during administration, which could require staffing adjustments as SCOmAb frequency increases. Most patients (6/9) expressed interest in home administration for potential time savings and flexibility, though concerns about training, support, and safety were common. Conclusions As SCOmAb utilization expands, facilities may face barriers associated with increased demand that could necessitate innovative solutions. To leverage the full potential of SCOmAb products, developers should consider how next generation product presentations might minimize identified pain points, streamline administration, and facilitate safe transition to home self-administration. Delivery device integration, whether through prefilled syringes, portable infusion pumps, or other delivery systems, may address current challenges but requires careful consideration of facility infrastructure, product complexity and usability, workflow impact, and patient training requirements.

Human–AI collaboration in Cyber–Physical–Social–Thinking (CPST) environments requires coordination among perception, reasoning, human judgment, and governance. This paper proposes Cyberlogic-enabled Thinking Space (CyTS), a conceptual governance-centric architecture organized through Entity, Mapping, Reasoning, and Governance layers. Its closed loop connects multimodal representation, heterogeneous reasoning, collaborative decisions, and controlled adaptation. The Entity layer provides operational descriptions rather than a sufficient ontology of cognition; logical consistency and predictive accuracy do not by themselves establish the causal validity of an action. CyTS therefore distinguishes associative, deductive, interventional, and exploratory claims and requires explicit assumptions, evidence provenance, uncertainty, and verification status at component interfaces. Structural causal models provide one implementable route, while equilibrium-based causal logic and proposals concerning brain–universe similarity and entangled machine thinking are examined as research perspectives with separate validation requirements. Governance mechanisms support privacy, accountability, human oversight, and runtime monitoring, including abstention when evidence or constraints are insufficient. Research hypotheses and evaluation protocols address causal transparency, decision quality, adaptation, cross-space coordination, and energy cost. Healthcare, education, and transportation scenarios illustrate the proposed workflow; they do not constitute empirical validation. CyTS contributes an auditable organizational framework and a testable implementation agenda, without claiming a completed theory of cognition or demonstrated performance gains.

This study examines how FinTech companies transform consumer behaviour data into financial value through artificial intelligence, predictive analytics, and hyper - personalisation. It explores how transactional, behavioural, and demographic data are collected, analysed,and converted into personalised financial products, recommendations, interfaces, and communication strategies. The study further evaluates how these practices influence customer retention, customer lifetime value, return on investment, average revenue per user, customer acquisition cost, and churn. Particular attention is given to machine learning, customer segmentation, recommendation systems, and predictive models used to anticipate consumer needs and improve engagement. The paper also considers the strategic role of data in product development, cross-selling, and marketing optimization. Alongside these benefits, it critically examines privacy, consent, algorithmic bias, cybersecurity, and regulatory compliance. The study concludes that AI-driven personalisation can create substantial commercial value in FinTech, but sustainable growth depends on transparent, secure, fair, and responsible use of consumer data over the long term.

Background: The rapid digital transformation of public services has increased the collection and use of citizens’ personal data, intensifying concerns about data breaches in government-operated systems. However, existing research remains fragmented, with technical cybersecurity perspectives receiving greater attention than governance and public administration perspectives. Objective: This study aims to systematically map global research on data breaches in digital public services from 2015 to 2025 and identify theoretical and governance gaps relevant to the Indonesian context. Methods: A systematic literature review guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines was combined with bibliometric and scientometric analyses of publications indexed in Scopus. Descriptive bibliometric analysis and author keyword co-occurrence mapping using VOSviewer were conducted on 1,169 open-access documents, while 62 articles meeting the final eligibility criteria were examined through qualitative synthesis. Results: The findings reveal an increase in research output and six thematic clusters. Cybersecurity and data security had the highest keyword occurrence (235), whereas privacy, ethics, and data protection exhibited the greatest total link strength (457). Governance, institutional accountability, organizational capacity, and public trust remain comparatively less integrated into technical cybersecurity research. Conclusion: This study reconceptualizes data breaches in digital public services as sociotechnical governance challenges involving technological vulnerabilities, institutional capacity, regulatory arrangements, and public trust. The findings provide a conceptual foundation for strengthening public-sector data governance in Indonesia while highlighting the need for empirical validation and further comparative research.

Growth hacking is often sold as a set of clever, low-cost tricks that any young start-up can use to grow fast. In earlier work, the author offered a reality check: growth hacking runs on data, and its core tools only start to work once a business has enough of it. This idea was introduced as Data Threshold Awareness, the eleventh meta-principle of the 10Ps marketing framework (Marketing Mix 3.0), with a provisional threshold zone of about 50,000 to 100,000 engaged users [1]. This paper puts that idea to the test through five complementary studies: 1. A simulation of 220,000 online A/B tests. 2. A recommender experiment on about 920,000 real film ratings (MovieTweetings). 3. A replication on about six million book ratings (Goodbooks-10k). 4. A simulation of an AI agent optimising a campaign. 5. A review of the early growth of five well-known technology companies. The studies all point the same way: data thresholds are real. A standard one-month A/B test needed about 62,000 monthly users to spot a 10% improvement in conversion reliably, and the value of each doubling of users rose and fell like a bell, peaking near 43,000. That number is not fixed: depending on a firm's conversion rate and the size of improvement it is looking for, the users needed ranged from under 10,000 to over a million. Personalised recommendations beat a simple bestseller list only after about 2,000 to 3,000 users in one dataset and 100 to 300 in the other, a gap largely explained by how active each user was. An AI optimisation agent captured less than a quarter of the available gain below 10,000 monthly users, but more than two-thirds at 100,000. The paper concludes that the data threshold varies with the task and is far steadier when measured in user interactions than in user counts. It closes with practical advice on how to grow before, during and after the threshold.

Digital technologies have increased the prospects for human interaction, economic productivity, and international relations. Digital technologies became stronger with the evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and social media. AI and social media are closely associated in many areas to enhance human flourishing. AI-generated deepfakes are widely circulated on social media, increasing their reach. Deepfakes have laudable roles in education and entertainment. However, they also raise significant ethical and legal concerns when created and disseminated with malicious intent. Drawing on doctrinal, descriptive, and analytical methodologies, this chapter finds that deepfakes are used to disseminate disinformation, gender-based violence, challenges to children, human rights violations, insecurity, and threats to international relations. It suggests that deepfake technologies must align with the ethical values of accountability, autonomy, human dignity, justice, privacy, and transparency. It also calls for amending the existing legal framework and promoting capacity-building programs.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Este artigo analisa a relação entre os direitos autorais e a inteligência artificial no ordenamento jurídico brasileiro, com foco no uso de obras protegidas no treinamento de sistemas e na autoria, proteção e responsabilização relativas aos conteúdos gerados. A pesquisa é qualitativa, bibliográfica e documental, de abordagem jurídico-dogmática e comparativa, com análise de legislação, doutrina, jurisprudência e experiências regulatórias nacionais e estrangeiras. Os resultados demonstram que não há vazio normativo geral: a autoria é atribuída à pessoa física pelo art. 11 da Lei nº 9.610/1998, enquanto a proteção de resultados produzidos com auxílio de IA depende de contribuição humana criativa demonstrável. As principais lacunas concentram-se na disciplina da mineração de textos e dados, na documentação dos conteúdos utilizados no treinamento e na definição de critérios para aferição da contribuição humana. Conclui-se que a dificuldade probatória constitui obstáculo central à tutela autoral, tornando relevantes mecanismos de transparência e proveniência, além do aperfeiçoamento legislativo em discussão no Projeto de Lei nº 2.338/2023. CHALLENGES IN PROTECTING COPYRIGHT IN THE CONTEXT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN BRAZIL: BETWEEN INNOVATION AND LEGAL UNCERTAINTY ABSTRACT This article analyzes the relationship between copyright and artificial intelligence (AI) within the Brazilian legal system, focusing on the use of copyrighted works in the training of AI systems and on issues of authorship, protection, and liability concerning generated content. The study adopts a qualitative, bibliographic, and documentary approach, employing a doctrinal legal approach and comparative methodology to examine legislation, legal scholarship, case law, and domestic and foreign regulatory approaches. The results demonstrate that there is no general regulatory vacuum: under Article 11 of Law No. 9,610/1998, authorship is attributed to natural persons, while copyright protection for AI-assisted outputs depends on a demonstrable creative human contribution. The main legal gaps concern the regulation of text and data mining, the documentation of content used in training, and the establishment of criteria for assessing human contribution. It is concluded that evidentiary difficulties constitute a central obstacle to copyright protection, highlighting the relevance of transparency and content provenance mechanisms, as well as legislative improvements under discussion in Bill No. 2,338/2023.

Background: Wetland rice cultivation requires effective inter-row weed management, but manual weeding is labour-intensive and conventional powered machines can be difficult to operate in puddled soil. Aim: To design and develop a battery-powered weeder that provides a lightweight, economical, ergonomic and eco-friendly machinery solution to reduce dependence on manual labour in wetland rice fields. Place and Duration of Study: Department of Farm Machinery and Power Engineering, SVCAET & RS, Indira Gandhi Krishi Vishwavidyalaya (IGKV), Raipur, Chhattisgarh, India, during 2025–2026. Methodology: The machine was powered by a 650 W DC motor paired with a 27 V, 30 Ah lithium iron phosphate battery system. Key structural components incorporated into the design included a mild steel chassis, rotating stainless-steel blades, a worm gear transmission system, a control unit and a dedicated floating mechanism. Results: The dimensions of the developed weeder were 780 × 560 × 1400 mm, with a total weight of 17.10 kg. Theoretical battery-runtime estimation indicated approximately 1.24 hours, while the ideal full-recharge time was estimated at approximately 2.4 hours for a 12.5 A charging current. The fabrication cost of the developed unit was estimated at ₹29,840. Conclusion: A lightweight ( ) battery-operated wetland weeder powered by a DC motor and a lithium iron phosphate battery pack was successfully designed, fabricated, and put into operation for inter-row weed management in puddled rice fields.

Human-centered AI (HCAI) and human-AI interaction (HAX) are increasingly important as AI adoption expands across high-stakes domains. However, empirical evidence remains fragmented across disciplines, limiting the development of transferable design guidance. This systematic review synthesized empirical research on HCAI and HAX and was reported in accordance with PRISMA guidance. Eight databases were searched, and additional preprint records were identified through arXiv. These searches yielded 9,718 records, of which 44 articles were included in the final review. Findings were organized around three dimensions: outcome metrics, collaboration frameworks and AI roles, and domain-specific patterns. Across studies, AI support was often associated with improved objective task performance, including accuracy, task completion time, and decision quality. Subjective outcomes such as trust, satisfaction, usability, and workload varied with transparency, explanation format, cognitive demand, and perceived control. Results suggest that HCAI and HAX frameworks should support task performance while preserving human autonomy and manageable workload. They should also support appropriate trust and reflect domain-specific needs.

Emergency Department (ED) visits for mental and behavioral health (MBH) conditions have increased, intensifying demands on psychiatric consultation, documentation, risk assessment, and care coordination. While AI systems integrating computer vision and Large Language Models (LLMs) could support ED MBH care, safe implementation requires domain-specific evaluation. This preliminary study conducted 17 scenario-grounded, semi-structured interviews regarding barriers, facilitators, and design requirements for AI-enabled consultation and documentation. Thematic analysis of 277 quotations identified 18 themes. Clinicians viewed AI as a beneficial clinician-in-the-loop support tool to reduce note-taking burden, improve information synthesis, detect behavioral cues, and enhance direct patient attention. Adoption depended on workflow fit, patient acceptability, explainability, and accountability. Key requirements included clinician review of AI outputs, ligature-safe hardware, standardized kiosk placement, reliable audio/ video capture, and fallback workflows for high-risk patients. Findings suggest AI systems be evaluated as embedded sociotechnical systems within ED MBH workflows, prioritizing workload, trust, safety, and legal accountability.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Embedded intelligence places sensing, inference, adaptation, and decision making inside physical systems limited by energy, memory, latency, cost, and reliability. This narrative review examines the field along four connected axes: hardware and software co-design, computational substrates, optimization at the model, mapping, and system levels, and applications in industrial automation, automotive electronics, healthcare monitoring, and the Internet of Things. Timing, safety, and security are treated as requirements that cut across all four axes. The review separates embedded intelligence from constrained on-device machine learning and from edge artificial intelligence, and it frames deployment as a cross-layer problem in which model quality, hardware mapping, timing, energy, security, and adaptation constrain one another. Two literature-based case studies, one on a field-programmable gate arrayand one on distributed microcontrollers, show how a gain at one layer produces a cost at another. A recomputation of the efficiency ratios reported in one of the studies shows why measurement boundaries and metric definitions must be declared. Six research priorities are derived from limitations that recur in the reviewed sources: lifecycle energy accounting, assurance of learned components, security of distributed deployments, reproducible benchmarking, portable deployment toolchains, and concept drift after deployment. Each priority is paired with a research direction and evaluation criteria for later studies. The evidence consists mainly of surveys, analytical studies, and laboratory implementations, so quantitative values are reported as stated in the sources, recomputed values are labeled as such, and approaches are not ranked. The proposed formulations and criteria are conceptual.

Background Digital health interventions have considerable potential to improve healthcare access, quality, and efficiency. Despite increasing adoption, many interventions fail to achieve sustainable implementation or progress beyond pilot phases because they are insufficiently integrated with user needs, organizational workflows, and health system contexts. Although human-centered design (HCD) has improved the usability and acceptability of digital health technologies, its application frequently remains confined to early design activities and is rarely integrated with implementation science throughout the implementation lifecycle. Objective This study aimed to develop a multi-level, human-centered design framework informed by a cross-project methodological synthesis integrating participatory design and implementation science to support the design, implementation, evaluation, and scale-up of digital health interventions. Methods A cross-project methodological synthesis was conducted using complementary digital health implementation studies undertaken in Kenya. The empirical corpus included studies spanning adolescent mental health, neonatal clinical decision support, digital health infrastructure, generative artificial intelligence, and frugal digital health innovation. Framework development followed an iterative analytical process combining thematic synthesis, constant comparative analysis, and abductive reasoning. The synthesis organized recurring methodological themes into an integrated framework spanning user, workflow, and system perspectives across the digital health implementation lifecycle. Results The synthesis identified recurring methodological processes that consistently contributed to successful digital health implementation, including contextual understanding, participatory stakeholder engagement, iterative refinement, workflow integration, organizational readiness, governance, and sustainability. These findings informed the development of a multi-level framework structured around six iterative implementation phases: Understand, Co-design, Prototype, Evaluate, Implement, and Scale, and three interconnected analytical levels: user (micro), workflow (meso), and system (macro). The framework conceptualizes digital health implementation as a continuous sociotechnical process in which sustained adoption and scale-up depend upon coordinated alignment among these three levels throughout the implementation lifecycle. Conclusions This study advances human-centered design by integrating it with implementation science through an empirically derived, lifecycle-oriented methodological framework for digital health implementation. The proposed framework may provide researchers, developers, practitioners, and policymakers with a structured approach for designing, implementing, evaluating, and scaling digital health interventions while supporting sustainable, context-responsive, and equitable digital health transformation.

Abstract Background In the growing field of interventional radiology, emerging technologies implement the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to help tackle growing demands for treatment. Due to the anatomical differences in animals, volunteers offer the most realistic training and testing scenario, however safety considerations restrict rapid prototyping of these new technologies. Simulators have been a key facilitator in the testing of new technologies among numerous medical engineering studies, but often lack the realism to reliably test AI. Purpose This proof‐of‐concept study presents methods to create or enhance hyper‐realistic radiographic simulators that can effectively function with a medical‐grade AI software. Methods Iron‐filled plastic was used to three‐dimensionally (3D) print a series of blocks of heights up to 30 mm. By analyzing the intensities generated by different thicknesses of plastic, anonymous fluoroscopic images were turned into height maps (lithophanes) and 3D‐printed. A static scene from transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) was then 3D‐printed and imaged with different presets using two different x‐ray systems for mathematical analysis. Lithophanes were then used as a radiographic background to experimental and commercial interventional simulators to test Caranx Medical's TAVIPILOT AI. Finally, fluoroscopies from 5 3D‐printed lithophanes were mixed with 5 real images and presented to 5 expert volunteers to establish their realism in a structured survey. Results The 3D‐printed x‐ray lithophanes test‐plates' radiographic appearance was rated as “Adequate” to “Good” across all fields of the survey, with participants praising their realism. The test‐plate was able to reliably recreate the TAVI scene in different x‐ray systems, with joint‐histogram correlation coefficients above 0.9, and global structural similarity above 0.8. The lithophanes were imaged as a standalone test plate and as a backing to dynamic TAVI interventional simulators; in both cases, TAVIPILOT AI responded to the simulator as if it was operating on a real anatomical image. Conclusions Lithophane plates present an easy‐to‐implement solution to recreate monoplane x‐ray scenes, which can be deployed to test software at the point of care with minimal logistical, ethical, or safety concerns. This study opens the door for a new range of interventional simulators able to recreate human‐like appearance to test AI, offering a non‐exclusive alternative to patient volunteers and anonymous data.

Abstract Background Serum uric acid (SUA) measurement is the direct basis for identifying current hyperuricemia (HUA). We developed a non-SUA screening model for situations in which routine occupational health information is already available but a contemporaneous SUA result is temporarily unavailable, delayed, or requires separate testing. Methods This cross-sectional study included 894 workers from 11 gas stations and related operational sites in Nanning, Guangxi, China. Current HUA was defined as same-examination SUA > 420 µmol/L in both sexes. Twelve prespecified non-SUA candidate variables were considered; total cholesterol was excluded because of high redundancy and multicollinearity with LDL-C, leaving 11 candidates for least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) screening. Internal validation used 100 repetitions of site-grouped five-fold cross-validation. Model performance was assessed using out-of-fold (OOF) predictions, discrimination, calibration, decision curve analysis, candidate screening thresholds, and bootstrap optimism correction. Results Among 894 participants, 169 (18.9%) had current HUA. Sex, waist circumference, triglycerides (TG), systolic blood pressure (SBP), and fasting blood glucose (FBG) met the prespecified selection-stability threshold and comprised the final model. The mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) across repeated site-grouped cross-validation was 0.858 (SD 0.004), and the pooled OOF AUC was 0.866 (95% CI, 0.838–0.893). The pooled OOF Brier score was 0.108, the calibration intercept was − 0.064 (95% CI, -0.322 to 0.192), and the calibration slope was 0.920 (95% CI, 0.791–1.077). At a 10% candidate probability threshold, sensitivity was 92.9%, specificity was 64.6%, and the negative predictive value was 97.5%. Conclusions The five-variable model estimates the probability of current HUA and may support prioritization of confirmatory SUA testing when a contemporaneous SUA result is unavailable. It does not replace direct SUA measurement or predict future incident HUA. Independent external validation is required before broader implementation.

Medical students increasingly engage with interconnected digital systems, health data, and artificial intelligence (AI), but existing instruments vary in the aspects of digital, data, and AI literacy they assess in medical contexts. This study developed and initially evaluated the Chinese-language Digital-Intelligence Literacy Scale for Medical Students (DIL-MS). Following two rounds of consultation with 16 experts, a 34-item questionnaire was field-tested at one Chinese university. Of 1118 returned questionnaires, 710 were analyzed in non-overlapping exploratory (n = 344) and confirmatory (n = 366) subsamples. Full-pool exploratory factor analysis and confirmatory factor analysis for ordinal data informed a revised 32-item scale across six domains: readiness, theoretical literacy, application skills, health data practices and interpretation, critical thinking, and ethical literacy. Parallel analysis suggested six factors, with some item assignments differing from the proposed domains. The correlated six-factor model fit better than the tested five-, four-, and single-factor alternatives, but absolute fit was limited (robust comparative fit index = 0.802; robust root mean square error of approximation = 0.090). Overall Cronbach’s α was 0.938, and domain α ranged from 0.726 to 0.871; convergent and discriminant validity evidence varied across domains. The DIL-MS provides medically contextualized self-report content for exploring perceived learning needs and mapping curricula.

Background University teachers’ occupational wellbeing and emotional exhaustion are relevant occupational-health concerns in higher education. As generative artificial intelligence becomes embedded in teaching work, AI acceptance may represent a perceived, context-specific appraisal of whether AI is usable for intercultural teaching tasks. This study developed a preliminary measure of AI acceptance for intercultural teaching and examined its cross-sectional associations with teacher resources and occupational-health indicators. Methods This two-sample cross-sectional study used Sample A to examine the empirical behavior of the AI Acceptance for Intercultural Teaching Scale and Sample B to test measurement validity and occupational health associations. IBM SPSS Statistics 27.0.1 was used for descriptive statistics, EFA, Cronbach’s alpha, correlations, and regression analyses. CFA and SEM were conducted in R 4.6.1 (lavaan 0.6.21, lavaan.mi 0.1.0, and mice 3.19.0) using robust maximum likelihood (MLR) estimation; CR and AVE were calculated from standardized CFA loadings, and HTMT from item correlations. Hypothesis tests used non-imputed scale-score regressions; multiple imputation (mice, m = 5) with D2-pooled CFA/SEM model tests served as sensitivity analysis, and indirect-association bootstrap intervals were sensitivity summaries rather than formal D2-pooled tests. Results The AITA items were suitable for factor analysis in Sample A (KMO = 0.940), but the exploratory loading pattern did not cleanly reproduce the theorized four TAM-based dimensions. In Sample B, the overall AITA score showed good internal consistency (alpha = 0.858), whereas the four subdimensions showed substantial overlap and weaker reliability and convergent-validity evidence. AI acceptance was positively associated with intercultural teaching self-efficacy and autonomous teaching motivation. Self-efficacy was associated with both occupational wellbeing and lower emotional exhaustion, whereas autonomous motivation was associated primarily with occupational wellbeing. Direct associations between AI acceptance and the occupational-health outcomes were not significant. Conclusion The present findings provide preliminary evidence for using the overall AITA score as a context-specific measure of AI acceptance in intercultural teaching. The results also show cross-sectional associations between AI acceptance and teacher-resource variables, but they do not establish causal effects, mediation, or intervention effectiveness. The four TAM-based dimensions should be treated as provisional content facets requiring further validation.
